title.value: UnMarker: A Universal Attack on Defensive Image Watermarking
UnMarker: A Universal Attack on Defensive Image Watermarking

abstract.value: Reports regarding the misuse of Generative AI (GenAI) to create deepfakes are frequent. Defensive watermarking enables GenAI providers to hide fingerprints in their images and use them later for deepfake detection. Yet, its potential has not been fully explored. We present UnMarker-the first practical universal attack on defensive watermarking. Unlike existing attacks, UnMarker requires no detector feedback, no unrealistic knowledge of the watermarking scheme or similar models, and no advanced denoising pipelines that may not be available. Instead, being the product of an in-depth analysis of the watermarking paradigm revealing that robust schemes must construct their watermarks in the spectral amplitudes, UnMarker employs two novel adversarial optimizations to disrupt the spectra of watermarked images, erasing the watermarks. Evaluations against SOTA schemes prove UnMarker's effectiveness. It not only defeats traditional schemes while retaining superior quality compared to existing attacks but also breaks semantic watermarks that alter an image's structure, reducing the best detection rate to 43% and rendering them useless. To our knowledge, UnMarker is the first practical attack on semantic watermarks, which have been deemed the future of defensive watermarking. Our findings show that defensive watermarking is not a viable defense against deepfakes, and we urge the community to explore alternatives. 2602 2025 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP)

Reports regarding the misuse of Generative AI (GenAI) to create deepfakes are frequent. Defensive watermark- ing enables GenAI providers to hide fingerprints in their images and use them later for deepfake detection. Y et, its potential has not been fully explored. We present UnMarker- the first practical universal attack on defensive watermarking. Unlike existing attacks, UnMarker requires no detector feedback, no unrealistic knowledge of the watermarking scheme or similar models, and no advanced denoising pipelines that may not be available. Instead, being the product of an in-depth analysis of the watermarking paradigm revealing that robust schemes must construct their watermarks in the spectral amplitudes, UnMarker employs two novel adversarial optimizations to disrupt the spectra of watermarked images, erasing the water- marks. Evaluations against SOTA schemes prove UnMarker's effectiveness. It not only defeats traditional schemes while retaining superior quality compared to existing attacks but also breaks semantic watermarks that alter an image's structure, reducing the best detection rate to 43% and rendering them useless. To our knowledge, UnMarker is the first practical attack on semantic watermarks, which have been deemed the future of defensive watermarking. Our findings show that de- fensive watermarking is not a viable defense against deepfakes, and we urge the community to explore alternatives. 1. Introduction GenAI has amassed popularity due to its growing so- phistication and accessibility [1], [2], [3]. This technology has solved problems in various fields [4], [5], [6], [7]. Y et, it comes with the risk of malicious entities using it to generate harmful images (deepfakes) [8], [9], proven by many reports of those being used in political smear campaigns [10] and non-consensual pornography [11]. Defenses first emerged as passive detectors [12], [13], [14], [15] that tell apart fake from real images, but these were proven ineffective, failing to generalize to unseen synthesis algorithms [16]. As training advanced genera- tors is costly and prohibitive [17] in the absence of the extensive resources and high-quality data that only a few GenAI providers possess, adversaries typically resort to these providers' APIs to generate harmful content. This recently led to the adoption of defensive watermarking as a countermeasure, which enables providers to embed hidden signatures in their images that can later be identified using designated detectors. Defensive watermarking has gained traction in the research community [18], [19], [20], [21], [22], [23], [24], [25] and the industry, as providers have already implemented and are testing such solutions (e.g., Google's SynthID [26]) or pledged to do so soon [27] in commitments to the White House [28]. Defensive watermarking protects against limited adver- saries, following the assumption that attackers lack the resources to train complex generators. Y et, existing schemes fail to demonstrate strong guarantees for this resistance beyond empirical robustness to naive manipulations. We devise UnMarker- the first universal (effective against all schemes), black-box (without access to the scheme's parameters or similar systems), data-free (no additional data needed) and query-free (without detector feedback) attack. Our motivating insight is that, for any scheme, there must be a universal carrier that embeds the watermark in all images. In layman's terms, this carrier is the set of all attributes the detector may examine when verifying the watermark. This set must exist and is finite (shared among all images) as detectors are computationally limited. By analyzing the desired resistance to basic manipulations and the requirement that watermarks must naturally integrate with various contents, we deduce that this carrier can only be in spectral amplitudes. That is, a “conventionally” robust scheme must construct its watermarks by manipulating the frequencies at which the different pixels vary, forcing the collective distribution of these value shifts at different rates to follow a unique pattern. We can roughly even isolate the range in which watermarks are encoded: the more robust semantic schemes [18], [24], which alter the structure, tar- get low frequencies while content-preserving non-semantic watermarks [19], [20], [21], [23] populate higher bands. UnMarker disrupts these spectral amplitudes. To remove non-semantic watermarks, it directly modifies the image to optimize a designated loss, affecting the rates at which individual pixels vary w.r.t. their neighbors and impacting the distribution of high-frequency amplitudes. For seman- tic watermarks, we devise novel optimizable filters and a procedure to learn their weights to systemically alter the consistency at different regions, causing discrepancies at lower frequencies. Unlike known filters that rely on geomet- 2602 DOI 10.1109/SP61157.2025.00005 ric heuristics, limiting them to minor distortions, UnMarker is guided by a perceptual loss to maximize the disturbance in visually non-critical areas without compromising quality. As a result, the carrier set is shifted away from the watermark's distribution. By targeting the carrier, UnMarker abandons the dependence on a specific model, leaving it successful without knowledge of the scheme or detector feedback. Previous adversarial attacks [29], [30], [31], [32], [33], [34] all face this limitation, failing under realistic conditions. We experiment with seven SOTA schemes from top venues. By combining the above techniques with mild crop- ping, UnMarker breaks them all, despite its black-box and query-free nature. We compare UnMarker with the recent VAEAttack [35] and DiffusionAttack [29], [31], [35], demon- strating far superior results, defeating semantic watermarks against which they fail and disputing misconceptions regard- ing these schemes' robustness to limited adversaries [29], [31], [35]. Our results urge vendors to rethink their response to deepfakes. We make the following contributions: • We thoroughly analyze defensive watermarking and reveal trade-offs that make it an invalid countermeasure. • We employ novel spectral optimizations to devise Un- Marker- the first universal data-free, black-box , and query-free attack against defensive watermarking 1. • We demonstrate UnMarker's efficacy against seven SOTA schemes under restrictive settings, rendering them useless. • We compare UnMarker to the strongest query-free black- box attacks, attaining superior performance and quality. • Using a novel class of optimizable filters to incur struc- tural disturbances, UnMarker is the first practical attack to defeat semantic watermarks, whose robustness has marked them as the ultimate candidates for trustworthy deepfake detection, showing this assumption is highly questionable. 2. Background & Related Work 2.1. Deepfake Detection Passive Detectors. These systems [12], [13], [14], [15] iden- tify deepfakes based on semantic incoherences [36], [37] and low-level artifacts [12], [14], [38], [39]. Advanced genera- tors can produce high-quality outputs without such telltales, and manipulations can fool these detectors [40], [41], [42]. They also fail to generalize to unseen models [16]. Defensive Watermarking. It assumes attackers lack the re- sources to train high-quality generators. A watermarking scheme consists of watermark (w), encoder (E) and detector (D).I na general-purpose scheme [19], [24], E accepts any image x and outputs a similar watermarked x w =E(x,w ). Given image x′, D extracts a sequence w′=D(x′) that will be almost identical to wi ffx′ was previously watermarked. Generator-specific approaches “watermark” generative mod- els: E can be the generator itself trained to only produce wa- termarked images [21], [22] or an algorithm that modifies its weights [20], [23] or latent codes [18] s.t. images it produces embed the watermark. Heuristics-based watermarks [43], 1. https://github .com/andrekassis/ai-watermark [44], [45] directly manipulate spectral representations, form- ing a signature in select frequencies. These are removable via post-processing [20], [30]. We focus on learning-based methods [18], [19], [20], [21], [22], [23], [24], [25], where E and D are DNNs as they resist post-processing. Semantic vs. Non-Semantic: Non-semantic schemes take an image and produce a visually identical watermarked version. Aside from StegaStamp [24], general-purpose schemes are non-semantic. Generator-specific schemes, ex- cept TRW [18], are also non-semantic, as their training restricts them to output images identical to non-watermarked references. Semantic watermarks can influence the content. This term was popularized by Wen et al. with their intro- duction of TRW [18] that alters the latent codes used by text-to-image Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs) [46]. When providing a random code with a textual phrase, the LDM uses this code as a seed to produce an image matching the text (e.g, “a dog on a bike” results in an image of a dog riding a bike but these objects will change based on the seed). TRW injects a pattern in the Fourier transforms of all latent codes before generation. As a result, watermarked images will differ from non-watermarked ones but still satisfy the text. This leaves watermarks invisible but highly robust. StegaStamp [24] precedes TRW and operates similar to its general-purpose counterparts. Y et, it is less stealthy, causing structural changes (see Fig 2). Still, its strategically distributed distortion ensures minimal visibility. In defensive watermarking, users cannot observe non-watermarked im- ages, further hiding these nuances and making StegaStamp highly applicable. While semantic watermarks primarily refer to TRW, previous work recognizes the similarities in both schemes, distinguishing them as more robust [29], [31], [35]. Thus, we refer to TRW and StegaStamp as semantic. 2.2. Attacks Against Defensive Watermarking Regeneration Attacks. Proposed by Zhao et al. [35], they rely on Diffusion Models (DMs) [47] or V ariational Au- toencoders (VAEs) [48] (henceforth, the DiffusionAttack and VAEAttack) to introduce noise and then reconstruct images after the watermark has been eliminated. Saberi et al. [29] and WA VES[31] revisit these attacks. All these works ver- ify non-semantic watermarks' vulnerability, against which regeneration attacks offer theoretical guarantees. Y et, se- mantic schemes remain robust. While TRW experiences some degradation [31], it occurs at a considerable distortion where the attack is invalid (see §3). Regeneration is the only practical ( black-box and query-free) attack but fails against semantic watermarks. It also relies on the denois- ing pipelines' fidelity, often impacting quality (see §6.2.3). UnMarker defeats all watermarks while also abandoning the dependence on regeneration models, ensuring quality. Adversarial Attacks. Realistically, attackers cannot access the scheme (see §3), making traditional adversarial attacks that target the decision boundaries of specific models in- effective. Thus, existing works make relaxing assumptions, failing to retain success under practical conditions. 2603
